title: Maharashtra FDA Seizes Rs 44.37 Crore of Food Stock in Diwali Drive, Suspends 326 Licences
excerpt: The October 15-November 3 drive covered 3,332 establishments; the wider two-month operation seized Rs 63.45 crore and suspended 954 licences across the state.
body:
• Maharashtra's Food and Drug Administration seized food stock worth Rs 44.37 crore — 1,886.44 metric tonnes — and suspended 326 licences and registrations in its Diwali drive from October 15 to November 3.
  • The drive covered 3,332 establishments, issued 1,501 improvement notices and collected 3,864 food samples, targeting sweets, khava, ghee, edible oil, dry fruits and spices.
  • The wider September 1-November 3 operation was larger still: 9,667 establishments inspected, Rs 63.45 crore seized and 954 licences suspended.
  • Buying Diwali food in Maharashtra? The FDA advises buying only from licensed shops, verifying the FSSAI number, and reporting complaints on its toll-free line, 1800 222 3365.

Maharashtra's festive food market has had its largest safety sweep of the season. The state Food and Drug Administration seized food stock worth Rs 44.37 crore and suspended 326 licences and registrations during a Diwali food safety drive conducted across the state between October 15 and November 3, according to the official statement reported by Urban Acres. The enforcement action covered 3,332 food establishments and produced 1,501 improvement notices, 3,864 food samples and 1,886.44 metric tonnes of seized stock.

What inspectors targeted

The drive aimed at products whose demand rises during the festival: sweets, khava, milk products, ghee, edible oil, dry fruits, spices and packaged food. Inspection teams covered sweet shops, dairies, farsan manufacturers, supermarkets, online grocery platforms, quick-commerce warehouses, hotels, restaurants, caterers, street-food vendors, fruit-ripening units and packaged drinking-water manufacturers. In Mumbai alone, the department conducted 1,037 inspections, issued 583 improvement notices, suspended 76 licences and began cancellation proceedings against four. The Konkan division recorded the highest value of seizures in the Diwali drive, at Rs 17.68 crore.

The wider two-month operation

The Diwali drive sits inside a broader statewide operation. Between September 1 and November 3, the FDA inspected 9,667 establishments, issued 4,603 improvement notices, collected 8,835 samples and seized 3,098.46 tonnes of stock worth Rs 63.45 crore, suspending 954 licences and registrations and initiating cancellation proceedings against 25, according to the statement reported by Medicare News. By commodity, edible oil (92.511 tonnes, Rs 16.31 crore) and salt, spices and condiments (89.532 tonnes, Rs 21.09 crore) accounted for a substantial share of the wider seizures, followed by milk products including ghee and khava (Rs 7.63 crore) and dry fruits (Rs 7.47 crore). Inspectors kept special surveillance on khava and mawa transported from other states, checking for adulterated or synthetic khava, cold-chain conditions and source records, alongside non-permitted colours, ghee and oil adulteration, expired products, incorrect labelling and analogue paneer sold as regular paneer.

What shoppers should do

FDA Commissioner Tukaram Mundhe said the administration would support honest businesses while taking strict action against those endangering public health, and the department noted that violations can attract penalties under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006, including imprisonment for selling unsafe food or operating without a valid licence. The FDA's consumer advice is specific: buy only from licensed or registered shops, verify the FSSAI licence number displayed at the establishment, and request bills carrying the shop's FSSAI number. Be cautious with unusually cheap sweets, khava, ghee and dry fruits, and avoid products with unnaturally bright colours, sour smells, stickiness or visible fungus. Milk-based sweets should be bought in small quantities, refrigerated and eaten within a day or two. For online purchases, check seals and expiry dates at delivery and refuse perishables that arrive warm, expired, damaged or tampered with. Complaints can be reported on the FDA's toll-free number, 1800 222 3365, or through its grievance portal.
